newsitem.title: USA: Texaco reaches settlement in bias case.
newsitem.headline: Texaco reaches settlement in bias case.

text.p: Oil company Texaco Inc. said Friday it reached an agreement to settle the discrimination lawsuit filed against it by about 1,400 black employees in 1994.
The plaintiffs' group said it was the biggest corporate race bias settlement in the United States.

As part of the settlement of the class-action lawsuit, the company said it agreed to pay the plaintiffs $115 million, along with a one-time salary increase of about 11 percent for current employees involved in the lawsuit. The raises will be effective Jan. 1, 1997.
The racial discrimination lawsuit charged the oil giant with systematically discriminating against blacks and denying them promotions.
"We have settled the case. We think it is precedent-setting," said Daniel Berger, one of the lawyers for the plaintiffs. "All I can say is we are very ecstatic."

In a letter to employees announcing the settlement, Texaco Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Peter Bijur said Texaco would increase the amount of business it does with minority companies. This would include advertising, legal, banking, investment management and accounting firms.
He also said the company "will actively work to increase the number of Texaco-branded stations owned by minorities and women."
"I have committed myself -- and the entire management team of this company -- to the elimination of any trace of discrimination in Texaco," he added.

The company also said it agreed to create an "Equality and Tolerance Task Force" to determine potential improvements in the company's human resources programmes, as well as to monitor the progress being made in those programmes.

Three members of the task force will be appointed by the plaintiffs and three by Texaco. There will be a mutually agreed-upon chair, Texaco said. Additionally, the company said, it will implement diversity, sensitivity and mentoring programmes.
"With this litigation behind us, we can now move forward on our broader, urgent mission to make Texaco a model of workplace opportunity for all men and women," Bijur said.
Texaco also said it would consider nationwide posting of openings for more senior positions than are currently listed.

The plaintiffs were to hold news conferences later Friday in Washington and New York. The Washington news conference was to be attended by civil rights leader Jessie Jackson, who with a coalition of other black leaders called Tuesday for a national boycott against Texaco until the lawsuit was settled.
